name: Artificial Intelligence

claims.claim_text: Onboard learning for aerial robotics is limited less by the algorithms than by resources: it demands heavy statistics plus enough memory to record flight data and process it in real time.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a lot of pretty hardcore statistics and no small amount of memory as well to, you know, to record all that data and process in real time.
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Where a drone has a fast telemetry link, the learning and heavy processing can be run on the ground station instead of onboard, with a self-contained airborne implementation being the harder ideal.
claims.quote_verbatim: It could be done on the ground, actually. And, you know, we have a relatively fast telemetry link
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: The Eliza conversational program was implemented in roughly forty lines of BASIC, showing that convincing dialogue behaviour could be produced with almost no underlying intelligence.
claims.quote_verbatim: And Eliza, I mean, was essentially 40 lines of basic back in those days.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bertrand Irrisou and Gerald Friedland of Audeme

claims.claim_text: A practising engineer's mental catalogue of parts covers cross-cutting facts such as an eight-bit microcontroller in a five-pin package that also carries an I2C output, a kind of lateral part substitution that automated part suggestion does not surface.
claims.quote_verbatim: that eight bit micro you're looking at in five pin packaging also has an i squared c bus output
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: One proposed route to a machine-learning auto-router is supervised training on thousands of known-good board layouts with substantial GPU resources behind it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Just show it like thousands of good board layouts and throw some GPU resources at it.
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Board layout quality is dominated by component placement rather than track routing, estimated at about ninety percent placement, so an automated router that does not solve placement addresses the smaller part of the problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: like it's 90% placement
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Machine-learning systems consume sensor inputs, which places electronics designers in the role of producing data that downstream decision-making systems can digest.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of what we're going to be doing in the future, I think, of the electronics world is making, making data that's digestible by the systems that then makes decisions based on them
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Low-cost single-board modules costing around eighteen dollars combine GPU-class silicon with camera input to perform machine-learning inference on board rather than in the cloud.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's basically on board processing with like GPUs and high end chips and stuff like that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The fast.ai course is an accessible entry point to machine learning for engineers without a data science background.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's called fast.ai.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Machine learning splits into an expensive rule-creation phase, exemplified by TensorFlow training, and a cheap rule-application phase that a small microcontroller can execute; the difference from hand-written expert rules is that no human ever knows what the derived rules are.
claims.quote_verbatim: And the TensorFlow stuff and so on, which is highly, which needs a lot of power. This is the creation of the rules. And then to apply the rules is very simple. So even a small microchip can apply the rules.

claims.claim_text: DeepPCB is a cloud auto-routing service marketed on deep learning that accepts KiCad board files.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a new deep learning artificial intelligence, wank wank, PCB routing AI software
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Claims that EDA auto-routers use artificial intelligence are not new; vendors have made the same marketing claim for around thirty years.
claims.quote_verbatim: because people have been talking about, oh, our new thing does AI and all that sort of stuff 30 years ago
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Most spatial-vision systems are assembled from two or three separate pieces, a neural accelerator, a general processor and a depth camera, whereas an integrated part combines the depth and inference functions.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the other solutions on the market right now are this kind of like two or three piece where you have some AI, you have some processing.
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Intel's acquisition of Movidius was aimed at the spatial half of machine vision, combining stereo depth sensing and inference on the same silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: And that's what Movidius is all about is, is having the spatial and AI.
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Depth-and-inference boards are designed so that retargeting a reference example to a different tracked object takes roughly three lines of changed code, and some products boot straight into a person-tracking demonstration.
claims.quote_verbatim: take our reference example, change like three lines of code
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: A domain expert can produce labelled training data by physically performing the event, for example repeatedly opening and closing a door while watching the sensor waveform, without understanding the data itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: just start opening and closing the door and looking at a waveform on a screen, you know, when you were closing and opening the door, right? So you can label that data without even knowing what the data is.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Conventional event detection forces the engineer to impose a mathematical model, such as fixed thresholds or slope detection, onto a natural signal and iterate by guess and check; a trained classifier instead starts from the desired output and derives the detector.
claims.quote_verbatim: But that's me imposing math on a very natural phenomenon and trying to make sure that my math fits it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: A machine-learning sensor proof of concept can be built for about fifty dollars, using a fifty-dollar development board with a free community edition of the model-building tooling.
claims.quote_verbatim: Cause our board is $50 and our sensible community edition is free.
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: The Skydio drone performs onboard obstacle avoidance built on NVIDIA processors, allowing it to follow a person through a forest while avoiding branches and twigs.
claims.quote_verbatim: But it's based on NVIDIA processes and it has so much AI that it can, you can walk through a forest and it will follow you avoiding all the branches and twigs.

claims.claim_text: Tesla's own position was that full self-driving requires a gigantic leap in artificial intelligence before it becomes viable, while the feature was still sold as an option for around ten thousand dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: We need. His own words. We need a gigantic leap. In. Artificial intelligence. Before. It's going to be. Really viable. Yet. He still. Will happily sell you it. For. $10,000.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A driving model is not a self-contained algorithm; it must be trained on large volumes of real-world fleet data, which is why Tesla built its own processors and supercomputer racks to run that training.
claims.quote_verbatim: The AI is not just a magic algorithm. It just works. It needs to be trained on real world data.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Training hardware pushes power delivery to extremes; Tesla's training racks were presented as containing one of the densest power supplies in the world measured in watts per square centimetre.
claims.quote_verbatim: Apparently they've developed one of the most dense power supplies in the world in, in like in terms of watts per square centimeter.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A characteristic failure mode of massively parallel training racks is intermittent dropout of individual processors among thousands, which disrupts the distributed job rather than crashing the machine outright.
claims.quote_verbatim: So one processor might just suddenly drop out for a bit.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Image generators reconstruct a subject rather than reusing the supplied photographs, and results degrade badly unless the input is a pristine photograph of a single person; human faces remain the weakest case.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's not like a, if it's not like a pristine individual, like photograph of one person, and even then it's still not that good.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Generated illustration was used in place of commissioned artwork on the basis that the output carries no royalty obligation, although the legal position on such licensing remains contested.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'd just spend a day throwing in random words into an AI art generator and then it pops out and it's all royalty free.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: In reverse engineering, the realistic contribution of a language model is recognising familiar code signatures, such as spotting that a block of assembly is a printf implementation or a Linux syscall, rather than explaining what unnamed variables mean.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I think it's going to be more of recognizing those patterns than telling you what it does.
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner

claims.claim_text: Mistakes in generated code are harder to catch than mistakes in one's own work, because the author of hand-written code has already formed a mental model of it and because the confident phrasing of model output lends the answer more weight than it merits.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because the way that they phrase things and the confidence that it has in what it's saying puts more, you know, more gravitas or weight on it than I think should be there.

claims.claim_text: A defensible use of a chat model in technical writing is breaking writer's block: taking its output as bullet points to research rather than as finished text.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm not going to use it to write, you know, an article for me, but if I need to think about some of the things that kind of is in the zeitgeist around a topic, like that might give me some bullet points that I could, you know, start to research
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Arduino's move into industrial control paired familiar Arduino programming with terminal-block termination and ladder diagram support, and the differentiator claimed over conventional PLCs was the ability to run tiny machine-learning models on the same controller.
claims.quote_verbatim: But see, the secret sauce is, like I said, you can add the artificial intelligence. You know, they got tiny, you know, machine learning.
claims.episode_title: Engineering Education with Dr Don Wilcher

claims.claim_text: Prompt engineer roles were advertised at between 175,000 and 335,000 dollars a year, with the work amounting to an internal audit of a company's own model behaviour.
claims.quote_verbatim: And, but the thing is it pays between 175,000 and 335,000 a year.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: An automated layout service treats machine learning as one tool among several in service of a finished, verified board, and accepts human intervention in the loop when the software struggles, since the customer bought a layout rather than an algorithm.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're not doing AI for AI sake. AI is just one of the tools that we use in ultimately serving that goal of like, get the board done
claims.speaker: Sergiy Nesterenko

claims.claim_text: Generated code still requires a competent programmer to integrate the pieces and verify the result, because models confidently report success on tasks they have not actually completed.
claims.quote_verbatim: You still need a good programmer to make sure the out, to combine it all together and make sure the output from the AI is good, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Useful competence with these tools does not require building or training models; knowing which tool suits which application and how to drive it is sufficient skill for most workplace needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if you just know which tools are applicable to which application and, and how to utilize them, that is more than enough skill.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The Raspberry Pi 5, with on-chip inference acceleration, performs roughly like a good laptop of five to eight years earlier, making it practical to ingest camera data, compress video and stream it from a small embedded board.
claims.quote_verbatim: the new Raspberry Pi five, it's now fast enough that it's, it's like what a computer was five or eight years ago

claims.claim_text: Training custom machine-learning models remains out of reach for most individual developers, who are limited to using models built by others.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're not yet to the point where everybody can build their own models for machine learning.

claims.claim_text: In a home automation stack, device control sits below a scheduling layer that handles priorities and external inputs, and any language-model layer belongs above that scheduler rather than in the control path.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think there is a potential layer above that. That's AI that might actually potentially someday.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The blocking failure mode for using language models in control applications is fabrication: the model invents events and states that never occurred and treats them as legitimate.
claims.quote_verbatim: The problem with AI at the moment is it just invents things. It just imagines things that aren't real.

claims.claim_text: Automated routing services such as Quilter are a useful incremental tool for board layout rather than general intelligence, and their value should be judged on that basis.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm excited about Quilter and other similar things, but it's just, it's a tool.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A consumer pool-cleaning robot sold on its intelligence failed to climb the pool walls, moved largely at random, and reset its own algorithm mid-run, with only partial mapping behaviour observed across repeated timed tests.
claims.quote_verbatim: The AI is not really much AI in it and it can't get up the walls properly and it's kind of random and it does sort of do mapping.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Pneumatic Tubes, Straight To The Home

claims.claim_text: FPGAs were initially expected to dominate machine-learning hardware because of their versatility, but GPUs proved better suited and displaced them for that workload.
claims.quote_verbatim: everyone thought at the start of all this AI thing, like many years ago, that FPGAs would be the future of AI because they're more versatile. And then everyone realized, no, the GPUs are better.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The economic argument against FPGA-based inference at scale is chip count and unit cost: the number of devices required makes FPGAs expensive relative to GPUs, which are themselves not cheap.
claims.quote_verbatim: Just the FPGAs would be so expensive comparatively. And it's not like the GPUs are cheap, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: NVIDIA's shift from the GTX to the RTX architecture made its consumer cards inference-capable, enabling a locally hosted assistant that runs on the user's own GPU and indexes the user's own files and video.
claims.quote_verbatim: They move from GTX architecture to RTX architecture. And all the RTX architecture is AI compatible, of course. And they've now released this new AI, which you can run locally on your GPU card.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Dedicated audio inference accelerators run a programmed model over a live microphone stream to classify background acoustic events such as typing, several people talking, a person shouting, or a plate being thrown.
claims.quote_verbatim: you will be able to detect somebody's typing. Somebody's talking to people are talking. One person is shouting. Somebody has thrown plate or whatever.

claims.claim_text: Custom hardware accelerators for image and audio processing are often commissioned as exploratory projects, built first and kept only if the measured benefit justifies it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because a customer wanted to do a hardware accelerator for some of their image processing and audio processing work.

claims.claim_text: Large language models themselves are treated as a commodity layer, with the unsolved and valuable part being reasoning over context, such as deciding which item in a calendar or inbox actually matters.
claims.quote_verbatim: All of this like LLMs or whatever is like interesting, but ultimately commodity.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Tools that claim to cut long-form video into viral short-form clips produced no usable output across repeated trials, a zero percent hit rate; the clips are correctly formatted but lack the editorial quality that makes a short work.
claims.quote_verbatim: it actually is 0% hit rate
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Voice cloning trained on a speaker's own recordings, including a guided online session reading prescribed words, produced unusable results across three or four different services.
claims.quote_verbatim: And I trained it with my voice. I even went through their online training thing where, you know, say certain words and everything.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The same practitioner who rejects generative tools for PCB layout found them effective for writing code, reporting that a coding assistant produced practically all of the code on a personal project.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're a very good tool. You know, you've got to, like, even when I did it, like, what, probably a year and a half ago now, it practically wrote all my code.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The work most exposed to language models is boilerplate text that nobody reads closely, such as legal contract language and filler marketing copy, where slightly worse output is still good enough for the purpose.
claims.quote_verbatim: boilerplate text for law, legal contracts. Nobody ever reads it.
claims.speaker: Lee Felsenstein
claims.episode_title: Lee Felsenstein: The Computer Revolution & Counterculture

claims.claim_text: Current systems do not originate ideas, and building genuine machine intelligence would first require defining and encompassing what real intelligence is, a task barely begun.
claims.quote_verbatim: It doesn't generate its own ideas. Cannot do it.
claims.speaker: Lee Felsenstein
claims.episode_title: Lee Felsenstein: The Computer Revolution & Counterculture

claims.claim_text: Intel's competitive position eroded on several fronts at once: TSMC pulled ahead on process, Arm and AMD pressed the server market, RISC-V grew from a small base, and the GPU and accelerator segment was ceded to NVIDIA.
claims.quote_verbatim: So TSMC kind of blew them out of the water on the process side of things. Uh, arm kind of took over some of the server, not completely took over, but AMD is nipping at their heels, arms nipping at their heels. Risk five is growing like crazy.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Data Provenance in the Home, Server, and Fab

claims.claim_text: The release of ChatGPT is the marker for the point at which the field entered public consciousness and companies began renaming products and businesses around it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can say AI really hit its straps when chat GPT was released
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Data Provenance in the Home, Server, and Fab

claims.claim_text: Language models answer well-trodden questions competently but cannot be asked to extend past the boundary of what is documented, because they have no knowledge beyond their training material.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want to push the boundary, then you can't ask it to push the boundary. Cause it doesn't know
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Vibe coding describes delegating the writing of code to a model while the human acts as product manager, supplying the specification and feedback on what works and what does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: Vibe coding is, like, letting the AI do the coding for you. And so, basically, you're basically, like, acting like a product manager.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A practical way to calibrate how much to trust a language model is to question it on the subject in which one has the deepest personal expertise, which exposes the limits of its answers.
claims.quote_verbatim: go ask AI about the topic that you know more about than anybody else in the world, or you've worked with extensively, and you'll actually find out how stupid AI is right now.
claims.speaker: Jerry Twomey
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: Taking a confidently phrased model answer on faith, without checking references, multiple sources and primary texts, is hazardous in domains such as signal grounding where established best practice governs the result.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it doesn't know anything about signal grounding and, you know, best practices, I'm, you know, if I'm taking it on faith and not looking at references and not looking at multiple sources
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: Assistants that scrape the web propose deprecated Zephyr APIs, because the RTOS evolves faster than the scraped material and has introduced new constructs such as hardware models; students are shown this failure in the second week of the course so they are not led down an outdated path.
claims.quote_verbatim: some of our AI tools that just scrape the web will take very deprecated, outdated APIs for certain functions and try to suggest that.
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: Gemini's web index was dated January 2025, an age that matters for fast-moving frameworks, and the practical outcome was abandoning language-model assistance for Zephyr work entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have functionally given up on Zephyr in an LLM.
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: For students who have not previously written C, assistants are useful for getting syntax close enough to what they logically intend, which lets them cross from intent to compiling code.
claims.quote_verbatim: This is where things like AI tools help is that as long as they have the ability to get the syntax pretty close for what they're logically trying to do, it helps nudge them over the line.
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: A concrete and modest use for a coding assistant is getting past the blank editor: producing something that at least semi-compiles, which the engineer then tweaks into working form.
claims.quote_verbatim: just give me something that at least I can like semi compile. And then, you know, I can go in and tweak to make it work.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Component and product discovery, historically done through web search and before that the new-products pages at the back of trade magazines, is shifting toward querying a language model with a specification such as an op-amp with given parameters.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the time people go to web search. I think that's starting to morph into using AI for that.
claims.speaker: Martin Rowe
claims.episode_title: The Measurement Blues with Martin Rowe

claims.claim_text: A purchase decision informed by model-supplied links was still settled by asking a known expert whose judgment could be trusted, illustrating that generated shortlists are a starting point rather than a source of truth.
claims.quote_verbatim: but I went to a person who I knew I could trust
claims.speaker: Martin Rowe
claims.episode_title: The Measurement Blues with Martin Rowe

claims.claim_text: Using generated data-gathering to assemble a corporate dependency map is a defensible application, since the alternative is manually reading hundreds or a thousand separate articles to trace the connections.
claims.quote_verbatim: that is something that you can use the AI for, you know, going out and finding all the dependencies with information and stuff like that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Time spent personally laying out a board and studying its schematic builds the mental model that makes hard debugging possible, such as tracing an unexplained result in an EMC chamber; delegating generation to a tool forfeits that context.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you just depended on AI to generate those things, I don't, you wouldn't have that context to, to be able to debug those issues nearly as much.
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: AI Tooling with Matt Liberty and Luke Beno

claims.claim_text: Converting an existing data centre to inference and training workloads required an entire additional building section devoted to power, on roughly the same computing floor area, with new trenched feeders and external transformers installed to supply it.
claims.quote_verbatim: But, because it's AI, they have to add on an entire section of the building just for power.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The additions to a converted data centre are dominated by cooling plant, power distribution and diesel generators rather than by extra server floor space, reflecting an order-of-magnitude rise in power density.
claims.quote_verbatim: And the stuff that added on, it looks like it's just for the cooling and power and diesel generators and all that sort of crap, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Asked to design a circuit, general-purpose models converge on the ESP32 roughly eight times out of ten, a bias that follows directly from how heavily that part appears in the online projects the models were trained on.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'd say, like, you know, eight times out of ten, it is going to tell you it's an ESP32.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: High-end imaging radar is moving to full lambda-over-two phased arrays with thousands of channels at chip scale, pulling real signals out of the noise, rather than to sparse compromise arrays whose gaps are filled by inference.
claims.quote_verbatim: This isn't like a computational, let the AI guess what the imaging looks like stuff. We're pulling signals out of the noise.
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: The Terahertz Frontier with Greg Charvat of Teradar

claims.claim_text: Modern phone cameras and large scientific instruments no longer capture an image directly; they compute one by averaging and combining many frames or datasets in software.
claims.quote_verbatim: whether it's not actually taking an image, it's creating an image, right.
claims.episode_title: Refrigerators and Robots with Amitabh Shrivastava
